title: Absalom Steals Israel's Heart, and David Flees
summary: Absalom spends years winning the loyalty of Israelites who come to Jerusalem for justice, then goes to Hebron under pretense of a vow and has himself proclaimed king. With the counselor Ahithophel on Absalom's side and the people's hearts with him, David flees Jerusalem on foot. On the way out he receives the loyalty of Ittai the Gittite, sends the ark back with the priests Zadok and Abiathar, prays that God will turn Ahithophel's counsel to foolishness, and sends his friend Hushai back into the city as a spy.
story: Chapter 14 brought Absalom home without justice or repentance. Chapter 15 shows the result. The son David longed for becomes the son who takes his throne. This is the heart of Nathan's warning that God would raise up evil against David from his own house (12:11). The chapter also turns David back into what he was before he became king: a man on the run, dependent on the loyalty of friends and the mercy of God. The flight from Jerusalem and the return in chapters 16-19 form one long movement, and the way David leaves (weeping, barefoot, submitting to God's will) sets the tone for everything that follows.
historical:
Absalom's rebellion shows real weaknesses in David's kingdom. The appeal of Absalom's words at the gate (verses 2-4) suggests that ordinary Israelites found it hard to get their cases heard by the king. Absalom's choice of Hebron was shrewd. It was the old capital of Judah, where David had first been crowned (2:1-4) and where Absalom was born (3:2-3), and some in Judah may have resented the move of the capital to Jerusalem. That even David's own tribe joined the revolt shows how deep the discontent ran.

The traditional Hebrew text of verse 7 reads forty years, which cannot fit David's reign; some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac translation read four, which the BSB follows. Ahithophel, David's most respected counselor, joins Absalom; as noted at chapter 11, he may have been Bathsheba's grandfather, which would give him a personal motive, though the text never draws the connection. Psalm 3, whose heading places it at this flight, gives voice to David's trust in God while his enemies multiplied.
cultural:
The city gate was where the elders sat and disputes were decided, so standing beside the road to the gate put Absalom where the aggrieved would pass. His chariot, horses, and fifty runners were the display of a royal heir (Adonijah does the same in 1 Kings 1:5). Normally a commoner would bow to a prince, but Absalom takes their hands and kisses them, a gesture of equality that flatters. A vow to worship at a sanctuary if God brought one safely home was a familiar kind of promise (compare Jacob in Genesis 28:20-22), and it gave Absalom a pious pretext to leave the city.

David's flight uses mourning signs: covering the head, walking barefoot, weeping. The Cherethites, Pelethites, and Gittites were foreign soldiers loyal to David personally; Ittai's six hundred men from Gath were Philistines. Priests could consult God for the king, which is why David calls Zadok a seer (verse 27). Crossing the Kidron Valley, just east of Jerusalem, and climbing the Mount of Olives took David toward the wilderness and the Jordan fords.
literary: The chapter has two halves: the conspiracy (verses 1-12) and the flight (verses 13-37). Hearts are its key word. Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel (verse 6), and David learns that the hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom (verse 13). The second half is a procession, as a series of people meet David on the road out of the city: his servants, Ittai, Zadok and Abiathar with the ark, and Hushai. Each encounter tests loyalty, and each is handled differently. The pace slows as David climbs the Mount of Olives, and the narrator lingers on weeping. David's speech about the ark (verses 25-26) is the chapter's spiritual center, and his short prayer about Ahithophel (verse 31) is answered at once when Hushai appears at the summit “where he used to worship God.”

outline.t: Absalom steals the hearts of Israel
The ark sent back to the city
David weeps on the Mount of Olives and prays
Hushai sent back to thwart Ahithophel

doctrines.note: David will not use the ark as a talisman to secure God's help. He sends it back and places himself in God's hands: “let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” He trusts God's sovereign will rather than trying to control it through religious objects.
David's prayer that God would turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness is short and specific, and he immediately takes practical steps, sending Hushai back. Prayer and prudent action go together.
David's flight is a season of humiliation that is partly the consequence of his own sin. He meets it not with self-justification but with weeping, submission, and trust.

words.note: Ganav, to steal. Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel (verse 6). The Hebrew idiom to steal the heart can mean to deceive, and both senses fit: he won their affection by deceiving them about himself and about his father.
Lev, heart. In Hebrew thought the heart is the center of the will and loyalty, not only of feeling. The contest between David and Absalom is presented as a contest for Israel's heart.

Chesed, loving devotion. David blesses Ittai, a foreigner, with the wish that the LORD will show him loving devotion and faithfulness (verse 20). Ittai answers with the very loyalty David wishes for him, echoing Ruth's pledge to Naomi.

Etsah, counsel or advice. Ahithophel's counsel will prove decisive in chapters 16-17, and David prays that it will be turned to foolishness. The story is partly a contest of counselors, and behind them stands God's own purpose.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter, but the Gospels place Jesus on the same road. On the night of his arrest he crosses the Kidron Valley (John 18:1) and goes to the Mount of Olives, where he prays in anguish (Luke 22:39-44), and where a trusted companion (Judas, as Ahithophel here) betrays him. Some interpreters see Psalm 41:9, about a close friend who lifted his heel against the psalmist, as a Davidic lament from a setting like this, and Jesus applies that verse to Judas (John 13:18). The parallel is thematic, not predictive: David leaves because of his own sin, while Jesus goes to the cross for the sins of others. But David's words, “let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him,” point forward to Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, not my will but yours be done.
questions: Absalom offered people what they wanted to hear to win their hearts. How can you tell the difference between genuine leadership and flattery?
Ittai, a foreigner, chose loyalty to David whether it meant life or death. What does costly loyalty look like in your relationships?
David refused to use the ark to force God's hand. In what ways are people tempted to use religious practices to control God?
